newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel economic reforms hard to implement-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Israel economic reforms hard to implement-analysts.

text.p: Analysts on Sunday welcomed the Israeli Treasury's proposal for structural economic reforms, while cautioning that they would be difficult to implement.
The analysts also sounded a warning against higher inflation and increased government spending.

"Structural reforms are difficult to implement," said Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets. "I am not that optimistic that most will be implemented. There are too many vested interests to really see the bulk of the plans implemented."
Trade unions alarmed by the prospect that their companies would face increased competition under the proposals have threatened to call a nationwide strike.
"But even if only part of the plan is implemented, and it depends which part, it will send a signal to the business sector that Israel is moving in the right direction," Katz said.
The cabinet on Sunday discussed the 1998 budget and the reform package but took no decisions.
The reforms, aimed at reviving growth next year, include steps for privatisation, capital market reform and foreign currency liberalisation.

Daniella Finn of Ilanot Batucha said: "At the moment what is most influencing the economy are interest rates and inflation. The fact that the Treasury is proposing leaving unchanged the inflation target for 1998 is not seen as friendly to the market."
The Treasury said the inflation target in 1998 would remain at the 1997 level of seven to 10 percent. The Bank of Israel favours lowering the target in 1998.
Shauli Katznelson, chief economist at Israel Discount Bank, gave a warning against encouraging growth by increased government spending.
"Everything done to increase competition and privatisation in the market is good," he said.

"But I fear the general atmosphere is that everything should be done to stimulate growth. The end must not justify the means. Renewed growth should not be attained by increased government spending or by a reduced cut in the government budget."

He also criticised the Treasury's proposal to keep inflation target at seven to 10 percent in 1998. "A higher inflation target does not lead to more growth because it will lead to higher interest rates."

The proposals include further liberalisation of the foreign currency market, although the Treasury did not give details other than to recommend that the central bank proceed towards making the shekel fully convertible by mid-1998.

The proposals set a minimum privatisation target for 1998 of four billion shekels ($1.1 billion), including the sale of the government's controlling shares in Israel's main commercial banks. Receipts would be used to finance debt.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had asked the Treasury to draw up a plan aimed at reviving economic growth, after rejecting its forecast that gross domestic product would increase by only three to 3.5 percent in 1998.
